findings.explanation: ATS is turned off app-wide, permitting plaintext HTTP and weak TLS to any host. Traffic can be intercepted/modified on hostile networks.
findings.remediation: Remove NSAllowsArbitraryLoads. Serve all traffic over HTTPS with TLS 1.2+, and scope any unavoidable exception to a specific domain via NSExceptionDomains.
findings.title: App Transport Security globally disabled (NSAllowsArbitraryLoads)
findings.why: NSAllowsArbitraryLoads removes the HTTPS floor for every domain, so any request the app makes over http:// or weak TLS can be read and altered on the path. Connections that use HTTPS stay encrypted, and the scan cannot say what, if anything, the app sends in cleartext, so confidentiality and integrity are scored low (convention point 2); the breadth - every domain rather than listed exceptions - does not change what is exposed per request.

evidences.value: ‎If you always allow access to your location, you can choose to share your live location, and it will update even when you're not using the app. If you only allow access while using the app, you can only send your current location or a nearby place.

findings.explanation: Persistent location access, including while backgrounded
findings.title: Requests permission: Persistent location access, including while backgrounded
findings.why: Always location declared: iOS can deliver location while the app is not in use, which is systematic monitoring (WP248 criterion 3) of location data (criterion 4).

findings.explanation: Either reads `kern.boottime` directly or declares the matching Privacy Manifest API category. Apple-documented as a strong device-unique identifier.
findings.title: Boot time fingerprint (PrivacyAccessedAPICategorySystemBootTime)
findings.why: Device and environment signals. On their own they meet none of the WP248 criteria; profiling happens in the SDK that combines them, which the tracker rules score.

findings.explanation: CTTelephonyNetworkInfo / CTCarrier, mobile country / mobile network code, used both for roaming detection and as a fingerprinting signal.
findings.title: Cellular operator information (CTCarrier)
findings.why: Device and environment signals. On their own they meet none of the WP248 criteria; profiling happens in the SDK that combines them, which the tracker rules score.

findings.explanation: Reads NSFileCreationDate / NSFileSystemFreeSize / NSFileSystemSize. Apple's Privacy Manifest specifically calls these out as fingerprinting APIs.
findings.title: File creation date / disk size as fingerprint signal
findings.why: Device and environment signals. On their own they meet none of the WP248 criteria; profiling happens in the SDK that combines them, which the tracker rules score.

findings.explanation: Low-level C call to read kernel-level hardware parameters.
findings.title: Imports sysctlbyname()
findings.why: Device and environment signals. On their own they meet none of the WP248 criteria; profiling happens in the SDK that combines them, which the tracker rules score.

findings.explanation: A privacy manifest declares required reason 1C8F.1 for the UserDefaults API: the code reads and writes defaults shared with the apps, extensions and App Clips in the same App Group. Apple permits this only within the group and forbids using it for tracking. Inventory: it shows a shared store exists, not what is stored in it. (The rule id is kept for continuity; it used to fire on any UserDefaults declaration and claimed an advertising-ID share nothing in the bundle showed.)
findings.title: UserDefaults shared within an App Group (declared reason 1C8F.1)
findings.why: Device and environment signals. On their own they meet none of the WP248 criteria; profiling happens in the SDK that combines them, which the tracker rules score.

findings.explanation: Imports CLLocationManager, basic location access.
findings.title: CoreLocation use
findings.why: Location data: WP248 criterion 4 names it among data of a highly personal nature ("location data whose collection questions the freedom of movement"). One criterion is a risk under GDPR, not a likely high risk.

findings.explanation: EKEventStore, calendars and reminders.
findings.title: Calendar / Reminders access (EventKit)
findings.why: A calendar is a diary, which WP248 criterion 4 lists by name ("personal documents, emails, diaries"). One criterion is a risk under GDPR, not a likely high risk.

findings.explanation: ABAddressBook or CNContactStore, phone-book access.
findings.title: Contacts (ABAddressBook / CNContactStore)
findings.why: The address book is other people's personal data, but WP248 does not list it among the high-risk criteria.

findings.explanation: Imports UIPasteboardOptionExpirationDate, the option that makes items written with setItems(_:options:) expire, so copied data does not stay on the pasteboard.
findings.title: Sets an expiration date on pasteboard items (positive signal)
findings.why: A positive signal: pasteboard items the app writes can expire.

findings.explanation: Imports UIPasteboardOptionLocalOnly, the option that keeps items written with setItems(_:options:) off Universal Clipboard, so they do not reach the user's other devices.
findings.title: Keeps pasteboard items on this device (positive signal)
findings.why: A positive signal: pasteboard items the app writes can stay on this device.

findings.explanation: PHPhotoLibrary / UIImagePickerController for photo-library access.
findings.title: Photo library (PHPhotoLibrary)
findings.why: The photo library holds personal documents and the location each photo was taken, data of a highly personal nature under WP248 criterion 4. One criterion is a risk under GDPR, not a likely high risk.

findings.explanation: UIPasteboard / generalPasteboard / UIPasteboardChanged, reading the system pasteboard. Background clipboard reads are a well-documented privacy issue.
findings.title: UIPasteboard / generalPasteboard access
findings.why: Access to a store of personal data. The contact list, pasteboard and media library are not among the WP248 high-risk criteria; photos and calendars are scored on their own rules.

findings.explanation: Direct reads from CMMotionManager / CMAccelerometer / CMGyro, used for gait analysis and behavioural fingerprinting.
findings.title: CoreMotion accelerometer / gyroscope
findings.why: Motion and touch input. Raw sensor access meets none of the WP248 criteria unless an SDK scores the person with it.

findings.explanation: LocalAuthentication / LAPolicy biometric checks. The app receives only success or failure, never biometric data. Whether the check is event-bound (MASWE-0020) needs the evaluatePolicy call site, which sits in encrypted code, so this records the API for review and is not a weakness on its own.
findings.title: FaceID / LocalAuthentication biometrics
findings.why: LocalAuthentication returns only success or failure; no biometric data reaches the app (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/localauthentication). Whether the check is event-bound and bypassable (MASWE-0020) depends on the evaluatePolicy call site MASTG-TEST-0266 reads, which FairPlay encrypts, so the rule records the API and nothing more.

findings.explanation: AVAudioRecorder / AVAudioSession.requestRecordPermission, direct mic recording.
findings.title: Microphone recording API (AVAudioRecorder)
findings.why: Recorded speech and voice messages are electronic communications, which WP248 criterion 4 names ("household and private activities (such as electronic communications)"). One criterion is a risk under GDPR, not a likely high risk.

findings.explanation: UIBackgroundModes contains "audio", keeps the app alive in the background. Music / podcast / VoIP apps need this legitimately, so it ships at low severity; pair with S04/S08 sensor rules to assess intent.
findings.title: Background audio mode (persistence channel)
findings.why: Camera and screen capture APIs. Capture alone meets none of the WP248 criteria.

findings.explanation: UIScreen.isCaptured / UIScreenCapturedDidChangeNotification, detects screen recording or AirPlay mirroring. Common in anti-fraud anti-remote-control flows.
findings.title: Screen-capture detection
findings.why: Evidence of a mitigation, not of the weakness: MASWE-0038 names missing capture-state redaction 'despite the platform providing an API to detect the active capture state' as the way the weakness is introduced. Observing the API is the opposite finding.

findings.explanation: AVCaptureSession / AVCaptureDevice, direct camera capture.
findings.title: Camera capture API
findings.why: Camera and screen capture APIs. Capture alone meets none of the WP248 criteria.

findings.explanation: Calls -[UIApplication canOpenURL:] or declares LSApplicationQueriesSchemes, used to test which other apps are installed (iOS analogue of Android's QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES).
findings.title: canOpenURL / LSApplicationQueriesSchemes runtime probe
findings.why: One canOpenURL call is not enumeration.

findings.explanation: LSApplicationQueriesSchemes names the scheme of a messenger, social or banking app (tg, vk, whatsapp, telegram, instagram, sberbank, alfabank, vtb, tinkoffbank), so -canOpenURL: can tell whether it is installed.
findings.title: Checks for specific messenger, social or banking apps
findings.why: Which apps are installed says what a person is interested in: WP248 criterion 1 covers profiling from "personal preferences or interests". One criterion is a risk under GDPR, not a likely high risk.

findings.explanation: The app declares URL schemes it can probe with -canOpenURL:, the iOS analogue of Android's QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES. A short list (deep-linking into a few partner apps) is routine; a long list is an installed-app fingerprinting signal.
findings.remediation: Trim LSApplicationQueriesSchemes to only the apps you genuinely interoperate with; probing a broad list to fingerprint installed apps risks App Store rejection.
findings.title: Probes installed apps via LSApplicationQueriesSchemes (31 schemes)
findings.why: Which apps are installed says what a person is interested in: WP248 criterion 1 covers profiling from "personal preferences or interests". One criterion is a risk under GDPR, not a likely high risk.

findings.explanation: Uses CoreBluetooth central-manager scanning (scanForPeripheralsWithServices), enumerates nearby BLE devices. Legitimate for accessory apps; broadly it maps the user's surroundings. Accessory / audio frameworks are allow-listed to reduce false positives.
findings.title: Bluetooth LE peripheral scanning
findings.why: Local radio and network APIs. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the API alone.

findings.explanation: Bonjour / NWBrowser usage hinting at local-network device enumeration (smart-home discovery, router probing).
findings.title: Local network scanning
findings.why: Local radio and network APIs. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the API alone.

findings.explanation: Reads the current Wi-Fi network info (CNCopyCurrentNetworkInfo / NEHotspotHelper / NEHotspotNetwork.fetchCurrent). The BSSID is a stable location proxy, the same access point identifies a physical place across sessions.
findings.title: Wi-Fi network / BSSID inspection
findings.why: The connected network's BSSID locates the device. Location data: WP248 criterion 4 names it among data of a highly personal nature ("location data whose collection questions the freedom of movement"). One criterion is a risk under GDPR, not a likely high risk.

findings.explanation: evaluateJavaScript: runs arbitrary JS in the WebView. Risk when source is server-controlled.
findings.title: Runtime JavaScript evaluation in WebView
findings.why: The app evaluates JavaScript in its WebView.

findings.explanation: Adding a WKScriptMessageHandler creates a JS→native call channel. Combined with a remote page, this lets a server invoke native methods.
findings.title: WKScriptMessageHandler JS→native bridge
findings.why: A JS-to-native bridge exists. What matters is what it exposes, which needs the two rules above to say.

findings.explanation: WKUserScript injects JS at document start/end on every load, useful for telemetry and credential interception.
findings.title: WKUserScript injection
findings.why: The app injects a user script into its WebView.

findings.explanation: WKWebView is the iOS embedded browser.
findings.title: WKWebView in use
findings.why: The app embeds a WebView.

findings.explanation: The app registers custom URL scheme(s) via CFBundleURLSchemes. Any app or web page can invoke these; if application(_:open:options:) acts on unvalidated parameters, this is an entry point for unauthorized actions. Custom schemes are also unverified (unlike Universal Links). Review the handler for input validation.
findings.remediation: Validate and sanitize every parameter in application(_:open:options:); never trigger sensitive actions from a URL without authentication. Prefer Universal Links (verified) over custom schemes.
findings.title: Registers 5 custom URL schemes (inbound deep-link surface)
findings.why: The app registers custom URL schemes. MASWE-0029 makes them a weakness when a sensitive flow relies on them or the handler does not validate input, which MASTG-TEST-0370 and -0371 read from the handler code.

findings.explanation: Legal iOS background-execution channels. `location`/`voip` enable persistent background execution and are the strongest signal; `audio`/`external-accessory` are moderate; `fetch`/`remote-notification`/`processing` are routine and declared by most apps.

metrics.modes: audio, fetch, location, processing, remote-notification, voip

findings.remediation: Declare only the background modes the app actually needs; each is reviewed by App Review and must map to genuine user-facing functionality, not background telemetry.
findings.title: Background modes declared: audio, fetch, location, processing, remote-notification, voip
findings.why: Background execution and push modes. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the mode alone.

findings.title: UIBackgroundModes contains "location"
findings.why: Background execution and push modes. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the mode alone.

findings.title: UIBackgroundModes contains "processing" (BGTaskScheduler channel)
findings.why: Background execution and push modes. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the mode alone.

findings.explanation: VoIP background mode keeps the app alive indefinitely.
findings.title: UIBackgroundModes contains "voip"
findings.why: Background execution and push modes. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the mode alone.

findings.explanation: com.apple.developer.usernotifications.communication entitlement.
findings.title: Communication-style push
findings.why: Background execution and push modes. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the mode alone.

findings.explanation: content-available=1 silent push lets the server wake the app to refresh data without a visible notification. The `didReceiveRemoteNotification` delegate method appears in almost every push-using app, so it's no longer a primary signal; the silent variant is the `content-available` payload and the `remote-notification` UIBackgroundModes entry together.
findings.title: Content-available silent push
findings.why: Background execution and push modes. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the mode alone.

findings.explanation: PushKit lets a server wake the app at any time without notifying the user, used by legitimate VoIP, but also as a covert wakeup channel. Apple has tightened policy several times; restricted to actual VoIP calls.
findings.title: PushKit VoIP push (silent wakeup)
findings.why: Background execution and push modes. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the mode alone.

findings.explanation: Opens a raw socket stream via CFStreamCreatePairWithSocketToHost / NSStream getStreamsToHostWithName. These APIs are not governed by App Transport Security, so TLS is opt-in, a common way cleartext traffic slips past ATS. Confirm the SSL security level is set.
findings.title: Raw CFStream / NSStream socket (bypasses ATS)
findings.why: CFStream and NSStream sockets are not covered by ATS. MASTG-TEST-0323 fails only when such a socket carries cleartext, which depends on whether the code enables TLS on it; that code is FairPlay-encrypted, so the scan records the API.

findings.explanation: A binary imports kCFStreamSSLValidatesCertificateChain or the deprecated kCFStreamSSLAllowsAnyRoot / AllowsExpiredCertificates / AllowsExpiredRoots keys, which exist to relax certificate validation on a CFStream socket. Networking libraries import them for optional settings, so the import shows the capability, not that validation is switched off.
findings.title: References CFStream TLS-relaxation keys
findings.why: The import shows the relaxation keys are referenced, not that validation is disabled.

findings.explanation: The bundle contains http:// URLs for 2 host(s): scripts.sil.org, www.apache.org. A hard-coded cleartext URL is a place the app may talk to a server without TLS. Whether it does depends on how the URL is used and on the ATS configuration, which blocks cleartext loads through URLSession unless an exception allows them.
findings.remediation: Switch each URL to https://, and remove any ATS exception that only exists to keep a cleartext endpoint working.
findings.title: Hard-coded cleartext http:// URLs (2 hosts)
findings.why: MASTG notes that an http:// URL in the bundle does not show it is used for communication; the scan records the candidates.

findings.explanation: References NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey / isExcludedFromBackup. The key does not guarantee exclusion, and sensitive files still need to be encrypted, so its presence is a reference, not a mitigation.
findings.title: Backup-exclusion API in use (NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey)
findings.why: Records that the app marks files as excluded from backup.

findings.explanation: A binary imports NSFileProtectionNone, the class that leaves a file readable while the device is locked. The import shows the option is referenced, often by a library that maps every protection class; whether it is applied to sensitive data needs the manual review the linked MASTG test describes.
findings.title: References NSFileProtectionNone
findings.why: The import shows the protection class is referenced, not that sensitive data is stored under it.

findings.explanation: A binary imports kSecAttrAccessibleAlways or its ThisDeviceOnly variant, the deprecated accessibility classes that keep a Keychain item readable while the device is locked. Keychain wrapper libraries import them to map every class, so whether an item is stored this way needs the manual review the linked MASTG test describes.
findings.title: References kSecAttrAccessibleAlways
findings.why: The import shows the accessibility class is referenced, not that an item is stored under it.

findings.explanation: Imports rand() / srand() / random() / drand48(), predictable PRNGs unsuitable for tokens, keys, IVs or nonces. Use SecRandomCopyBytes or arc4random_buf. `arc4random() % n` also introduces modulo bias; prefer arc4random_uniform(n).
findings.title: Non-cryptographic random number generator
findings.why: A non-cryptographic generator is linked. MASTG-TEST-0311 fails only when its output is used for keys, tokens or other security values, which is in FairPlay-encrypted code, so the scan records the API.

findings.explanation: Imports CC_MD5 / CC_SHA1 (CommonCrypto) or CryptoKit's Insecure.MD5 / Insecure.SHA1. Both are collision-broken and unsuitable for signatures, integrity checks or password hashing, but are also widely used for non-security purposes (cache keys, ETags, file checksums), so the finding is a pointer for review.
findings.title: Weak hash primitive (MD5 / SHA-1)
findings.why: MD5 or SHA-1 is linked. MASTG-TEST-0211 fails only when the hash protects sensitive data; checksums and cache keys pass. That use is in FairPlay-encrypted code, so the scan records the API.

findings.explanation: Binaries carrying 16076 debugger (stab) entries in their symbol table: WatchServiceExtension.appex. Stabs name source files, object files and functions, and often the build machine's paths. They make reverse engineering easier and are not needed to run the app.
findings.remediation: Set Debug Information Format to DWARF with dSYM File for release builds and keep the dSYM out of the app bundle; strip the binaries.
findings.title: Debug symbols left in binaries (1)
findings.why: Leftover debug information eases reverse engineering; MASWE files it under the resilience profile, where it is a finding only when resilience is required.

findings.explanation: application-groups entitlement allows multiple apps from the same publisher to share UserDefaults/files (often used to share IDFA / VPN-detected flag between sibling apps).
findings.title: App Groups entitlement (cross-app data sharing)
findings.why: Shared container between the vendor's own apps.

findings.explanation: aps-environment entitlement, push notifications.
findings.title: APS push environment
findings.why: Push environment the build targets.

findings.explanation: The binary imports dlopen/dlsym, so it can resolve and call code chosen at runtime rather than at link time. That is how optional frameworks, plugin architectures and A/B-tested SDKs are loaded, and it is entirely normal, so this ships as INFO inventory rather than a weakness. It matters only as context: an app that also carries obfuscation (SURV-04) or a data broker (TRK-02) can assemble behaviour a static scan cannot see, and dynamic code loading is the mechanism that makes that possible. Note the limit of the signal: an import proves the symbol is linked, not that it is ever called, and iOS forbids loading code that is not already in the signed bundle. (MASWE-0049)
findings.title: Dynamic loader in use (dlopen / dlsym)
findings.why: dlopen/dlsym are present in the binary.

findings.explanation: com.apple.developer.associated-domains, handles universal links / web credentials.
findings.title: Associated domains / universal links
findings.why: Associated domains the app claims.

findings.explanation: Imports SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags, which binds a Keychain item or key to user presence, biometrics or the device passcode. A positive signal; which flags are passed cannot be read from the symbol table.
findings.title: Keychain access control in use (SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags)
findings.why: A positive signal: Keychain items are access-control bound.

findings.explanation: Uses the Keychain Services API (SecItemAdd / SecItemCopyMatching / SecItemUpdate). Informational, pair with SECH-02.keychain_accessible_always to judge whether items are protected with an appropriate accessibility / access-control class.
findings.title: Keychain API in use (SecItem)
findings.why: A positive signal: the app uses the Keychain.

findings.explanation: Info.plist records MinimumOSVersion 15.1, the iOS 26.5 SDK (iphoneos26.5) and Xcode 26.6. The minimum decides which platform protections the app can count on; the SDK decides which current platform behaviour it opts into.
findings.title: Supports iOS 15.1 and later; built with the iOS 26.5 SDK
findings.why: Records the minimum iOS version and the SDK the app was built with.

findings.explanation: Imports the C function getifaddrs() which lists every network interface. NOTE: getifaddrs is also the standard primitive for plain reachability and local-IP discovery and is linked by many networking SDKs, so the import alone is a weak VPN signal that fires on most apps. MASTG / privacy-guide VPN detection keys on NEVPNManager or an explicit tunnel-interface name (utun/ppp/ipsec), kept here as an informational marker only.
findings.title: Imports getifaddrs() for network interface enumeration
findings.why: Reading network interfaces and proxy settings on the device meets none of the WP248 criteria by itself.

findings.explanation: Calls CFNetworkCopySystemProxySettings or reads HTTP proxy keys, often used to detect that the user has interception/SOCKS/HTTP proxy enabled.
findings.title: Reads system proxy settings
findings.why: Reading network interfaces and proxy settings on the device meets none of the WP248 criteria by itself.

findings.explanation: Calls _dyld_image_count / _dyld_get_image_name, can be used to detect injected dylibs (tweaks, Frida gadget). NOTE: these symbols are also used by crash reporters, analytics SDKs and the Swift runtime to enumerate loaded images, so bare presence is not anti-analysis. OWASP MASTG anti-debugging tests key on ptrace / sysctl(P_TRACED) rather than dyld enumeration, so this is an informational capability marker, not a weakness.
findings.title: dyld image-list introspection

findings.explanation: Calls fork() or posix_spawn(), calling these from a sandboxed iOS app is forbidden; a successful call indicates a jailbroken environment. NOTE: many cross-platform SDKs and the Swift/ObjC runtime merely *link* these symbols without calling them on iOS, so the import alone is a very weak signal and fires on most apps. Treated as informational rather than a weakness (MASTG keys anti-tamper on ptrace / sysctl, not on linked posix symbols).
findings.title: fork / posix_spawn execution probe

findings.explanation: UIBackgroundModes contains "fetch", system schedules periodic background wake-ups for opportunistic data sync. "processing", "remote-notification" and "voip" are covered by S12 (system persistence) and S19 (push channels).
findings.title: Background fetch mode (UIBackgroundModes "fetch")

findings.explanation: BGTaskScheduler / submitTaskRequest, schedules periodic background wake-ups, used to drain accumulated logs/telemetry while the user is away.
findings.title: BGTaskScheduler silent background wake-ups

findings.explanation: Across the bundle's privacy manifests the app and its SDKs declare collecting: AdvertisingData, CoarseLocation, Contacts, CrashData, CustomerSupport, DeviceID, EmailAddress, OtherDiagnosticData, OtherUserContent, PaymentInfo, PerformanceData, PhoneNumber, ProductInteraction, PurchaseHistory, SearchHistory, UserID. 15 are declared linked to the user's identity and 0 used for tracking. This is what the developer states; a static scan cannot show what leaves the device.

metrics.types: AdvertisingData, CoarseLocation, Contacts, CrashData, CustomerSupport, DeviceID, EmailAddress, OtherDiagnosticData, OtherUserContent, PaymentInfo, PerformanceData, PhoneNumber, ProductInteraction, PurchaseHistory, SearchHistory, UserID

findings.title: Privacy manifests declare 16 collected data types
findings.why: Records what the developer declares; the declaration is not a defect.

findings.explanation: Uses Apple's Declared Age Range API, a privacy-preserving age-assurance signal (the app learns an age band without collecting a birthdate).
findings.title: Declared Age Range API in use
findings.why: The app calls the DeclaredAgeRange API. Asking the platform for an age band, rather than guessing, is the app doing the right thing.

findings.explanation: The app declares com.apple.developer.declared-age-range, Apple's API for asking the system for a user's age bracket without collecting a birth date. Using it is the privacy-preserving way to age-gate, so this is a positive signal reported as inventory.
findings.title: Declared Age Range entitlement (positive disclosure signal)
findings.why: The app declares an age range. A declaration is the app being transparent, not a gap.

findings.explanation: The bundle references 14 endpoint(s) whose owner is based in US, owners: Apple, Google, Meta. The country is the owning organisation's home jurisdiction from the tracker database, not where a server is hosted, and a referenced endpoint is not observed traffic. If the app sends personal data there, it is a third-country transfer: whether that is lawful depends on the safeguards, purpose and paperwork behind it, none of which is visible in a binary. US holds no EU adequacy decision, so a transfer there needs an Art. 46 safeguard or an Art. 49 derogation.

metrics.adequacyNote: US holds no EU adequacy decision, so a transfer there needs an Art. 46 safeguard or an Art. 49 derogation.

findings.title: Endpoints owned by US-based organisations (14 endpoints)
findings.why: Where the endpoint owner is registered. International transfer is GDPR Chapter V, not a WP248 criterion.

findings.explanation: Uses on-device ML (CoreML / Foundation Models) with no detected cloud AI endpoint, a privacy-preserving posture.
findings.title: On-device ML only (no cloud AI endpoint)
findings.why: On-device inference sends nothing. It is the opposite of the rest of TRK-05.

findings.explanation: The main Mach-O is encrypted by the App Store. Static string scanning of its TEXT segment won't work without a decrypted dump (e.g., via frida-ios-dump or bagbak on a jailbroken device). Embedded frameworks and dylibs are USUALLY ENCRYPTED TOO (measured 91% across the reference corpus; in half of apps every Mach-O is encrypted), so TEXT-segment string recall is limited bundle-wide, not just for the main binary. What still survives encryption is __LINKEDIT: symbols, imported/defined symbol names, ObjC selectors and linked dylibs, which is why symbol-based detection carries this scan rather than string matching.
findings.remediation: For full TEXT-segment coverage, supply a decrypted .ipa produced by frida-ios-dump or bagbak from a jailbroken device. Resource files, plists, entitlements, symbols, selectors and linked dylibs are still scanned in the meantime.
findings.title: Main executable is FairPlay-encrypted
findings.why: Scan metadata: what the scanner could and could not see.
